pedagogy.summary: Comparing and ordering unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (2/5, 4/5) is the procedure that operationalises fraction magnitude. Two rules that FEEL contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a larger denominator means a SMALLER fraction (more equal parts, each smaller), while for same-denominator fractions a larger numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized part). Teach both with bars/number lines so the direction of each rule is grounded in piece size, and so children don't over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.
bestPractices: Order unit fractions against a common whole using aligned bars so 1/5 is visibly the smallest and 1/2 the largest
Use a 'cut into more pieces' action so children feel each piece shrink as the denominator grows
Order same-denominator fractions by counting how many of the SAME piece, keeping the piece size fixed
Place fractions on a shared number line so both comparisons are read as position
Make explicit WHY the denominator direction flips between the two cases (piece size vs how many pieces)
keyRepresentations: Aligned equal-length bars for unit fractions (a fraction wall column)
Number line locating the fractions being compared
Same-denominator strip where only the count of shaded parts changes
'Cut into more' animation shrinking each unit fraction
commonMisconceptions: Whole-number bias — orders unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 (bigger denominator judged bigger)
Over-correction — after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses same-denominator fractions too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5)
Compares numerators and denominators independently rather than as one quantity
Cannot place the fractions consistently on a number line to check the order
Ignores that the whole must be the same when comparing

learn.summary: Year 3 learners (age 7-8) compare and order unit fractions (1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5) and same-denominator fractions (1/5...4/5). Two directions that feel contradictory must be held together: for unit fractions a LARGER denominator means a SMALLER fraction (the whole is cut into more, smaller pieces), while for same-denominator fractions a LARGER numerator means a LARGER fraction (more of the same-sized piece). These are not one rule reversing; they compare different varying quantities. Ground both in piece size using aligned bars and a shared number line so children do not over-generalise a blanket 'bigger bottom = smaller'.

activities.title: Order unit fractions under one shared whole
feedback: If a learner puts 1/5 first and 1/2 last (whole-number bias), lay the unit fractions as aligned bars against ONE whole so 1/5 is visibly the shortest; ask them to point to which piece is largest.
Probe: 'You put 1/2 first. Show me on the bars (for example, equal pizzas cut into halves and fifths) WHY one half is bigger than one fifth.'
If pieces are not aligned to a common whole, redraw them under the same '1 whole' rule before comparing, and remind that the represented whole must be the same to compare the portions.
activities.rationale: Grounding fraction magnitude in part size against a common whole targets whole-number bias when ordering unit fractions.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Take fraction cards 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 and arrange them from largest to smallest.

Represent each card as a bar the same length as a single common '1 whole' bar, split into that many equal parts with one part shaded, and line the bars up beneath that '1 whole' so the shaded pieces can be compared by length.
State and check the order: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest, confirming 1/5 is the shortest and 1/2 the longest.
Explain out loud why 1/2 is bigger than 1/5 by pointing at the piece lengths against the same whole.
activities.intendedInsight: When the whole is the same, a unit fraction with a larger denominator is smaller because the whole is split into more, smaller pieces.

activities.title: Cut into more pieces and feel each one shrink
feedback: Probe: 'Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? If I cut a cake into more and more pieces, what happens to the size of each piece?'
If a learner still judges more pieces as bigger, slow the cutting down and compare one piece before and after an extra cut on the same whole.
An optional 'cut into more' action or animation that adds a slice and visibly shrinks every piece makes the shrinking concrete; this is one way to show it, not the only way.
activities.rationale: An enacted partitioning action ties the abstract denominator rule to a felt change in piece size, reinforcing more-parts-means-smaller.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
learnerActions: Start with one whole and partition it into 2, then 3, then 4, then 5 equal pieces, each time comparing the size of a single piece to the previous one.
Describe what happens to the size of each piece as more cuts are added.
Connect the action back to the cards: more pieces (bigger denominator) means each piece, and so each unit fraction, is smaller.
activities.intendedInsight: Cutting a fixed whole into more equal parts makes each part smaller, so more pieces means a smaller unit fraction.

activities.title: Order same-denominator fractions by counting the same-sized piece
feedback: If a learner reverses the fifths (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5 > 4/5) after learning 'bigger bottom = smaller' (over-correction), fix the piece size at one fifth and count how many are shaded; show 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.

Probe: 'Why does "more fifths" mean MORE, but a bigger bottom number mean LESS?' Separate 'how big each piece is' from 'how many pieces there are' — the unit-fraction case varies the piece size, this case varies the count.
Reinforce that here the piece size does NOT change; only the count of shaded pieces does.
activities.rationale: Holding the piece fixed while varying the count isolates the numerator's meaning and guards against over-generalising the denominator rule to same-denominator sets.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Take fifths fractions 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5 and order them from largest to smallest, keeping the piece size (one fifth) fixed.
Represent each as a bar where only the number of shaded fifths changes, and check that 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5.
State the order 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 and explain that more fifths means more because each piece is the same size.
activities.intendedInsight: When the denominator is fixed, the numerator counts how many of the same-sized piece, so a larger numerator means a larger fraction.

activities.title: Place and read the fractions on a shared number line
feedback: Probe: 'Where would 3/5 sit compared to 1/2 on the line, bigger or smaller? How could the number line help you decide?'
If a learner compares numerators and denominators independently (component comparison), insist on one quantity per card and order by position on the line.
If 1/5 is placed furthest right, revisit the unit-fraction bars before returning to the line.
activities.rationale: A shared number line represents each fraction as a single quantity, countering component comparison and letting learners self-check both orderings against position.
sourceClaims: Students frequently show whole-number bias when ordering fractions, viewing those with larger denominators as larger (e.g. 1/8 > 1/3); this can be diagnosed by having them label and compare fractions, and remedied by grounding magnitude in the number line and part size.
learnerActions: Place each fraction from both sets onto one shared number line between 0 and 1, consistent with its order.
Decide where 3/5 sits compared with 1/2 and judge whether it is bigger or smaller.
Use position on the line to check that the unit-fraction order and the fifths order agree with where each fraction lands.

Try a mixed set (e.g. 1/5, 1/2, 3/5) and use positions on the number line, together with the two rules, to order it; note that neither rule on its own can compare fractions such as 3/5 and 1/2, where both the numerator and the denominator differ.
activities.intendedInsight: Both comparisons can be read as position on one number line, which unifies the unit-fraction and same-denominator cases into a single idea of magnitude.

activities.title: Practise and check the orderings
feedback: For 2/5 vs 4/5, confirm 4/5 is larger because it has more fifths; if a learner instead picks 2/5 (over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' where the denominators are equal), return to the fixed-piece bar and count the shaded fifths.

Checking whether the order is correct is useful, but build the underlying magnitude sense first with bars and the number line, since simply recognising the right answer does not by itself elicit the reasoning.
Ask the learner to justify each answer so correct ordering is backed by the piece-size explanation, not a memorised rule.
activities.rationale: Targeted practice can consolidate ordering and reveal whole-number bias or over-correction. Ask for a piece-size or number-line explanation alongside the selected or ordered answer.
sourceClaims: Year 3 pupils compare and order unit fractions, and fractions with the same denominators.
learnerActions: Order 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 from largest to smallest as an ordering task.

Compare 2/5 and 4/5 and choose the larger, explaining the choice; be alert to the tempting wrong answer of picking 2/5 by over-applying 'bigger bottom = smaller' to a comparison where only the numerator differs.
Place a given fraction at the right spot on a number line as a final check.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent, correct ordering of both fraction types, with the reasoning articulated, confirms the magnitude idea has taken hold.

constraints: When comparing fractions with bars or area representations, the represented whole must be the same; aligned bars and number-line placements only work when they share one unit. As numbers, fractions still have comparable magnitudes (e.g. by position on a shared number line).
A static fraction wall or reference image lets children read off comparisons but does not let them enact the ordering, so use it as a reference scaffold alongside, not instead of, hands-on ordering.
Recognition or multiple-choice practice checks whether the order is correct but does not by itself require the learner to construct and justify the ordering; pair it with explanation.

Keep the two cases explicitly connected: unit-fraction comparison varies the denominator (numerator fixed at 1), while same-denominator comparison varies the numerator (denominator fixed) — explain that they compare different quantities, which is why 'bigger bottom = smaller' must not be over-generalised to same-denominator sets. This is not a single rule flipping.
Fraction comparison here uses lengths of bars and positions on a number line (or areas of equal wholes); for this objective a third spatial dimension adds no comparative information.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed a static image 'can't let them ACT the ordering' and that dialogue is poor for this procedure; these have been softened to scoped limits (a static reference supports reading-off but not enacting) rather than universal laws, since the sources do not establish comparative efficacy or necessity.

Optional interaction examples (drag-to-unfurl bars, a 'cut into more' action, fifths bars growing, placement on a line) are retained as concrete ways to make the mechanism visible; they are illustrative, not mandatory.

The original pedagogy and quiz task described the denominator rule as 'flipping' between the two cases and referenced a 'larger-denominator distractor' for 2/5 vs 4/5; both are incoherent (the cases vary different quantities; 2/5 and 4/5 share denominator 5) and have been corrected rather than reproduced.

Self-audit of the arithmetic and ordering logic found the source orderings correct: unit fractions largest-to-smallest 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5; fifths largest-to-smallest 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5; 4/5 > 2/5. No conceptual errors were introduced into learner-facing actions.

probeDeeper: You put 1/2 first. Show me on the pizzas WHY one half is bigger than one fifth.
Which is bigger, 1/3 or 1/4? If I cut a cake into more and more pieces, what happens to the size of each piece?
You ordered the fifths 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5. Why does 'more fifths' mean MORE, but a bigger bottom number mean LESS?
Where would 3/5 sit compared to 1/2 on the line — bigger or smaller? How could the number line help you decide?
assess.correctAnswer: Unit fractions largest→smallest: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 (larger denominator = smaller piece). Same-denominator fractions largest→smallest: 4/5, 3/5, 2/5, 1/5 (more fifths = more). Each card placed consistently on the number line matching its order.

errorPatterns.pattern: Whole-number bias on unit fractions — orders 1/5 > 1/4 > 1/3 > 1/2, treating the larger denominator as the larger fraction
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lay the unit fractions as aligned bars against one whole so 1/5 is visibly smallest; cut a whole into more pieces to feel each shrink; reteach more-parts-means-smaller
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Puts 1/5 first and 1/2 last, or places 1/5 furthest right on the number line

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-correction — having learned 'bigger bottom = smaller', reverses the same-denominator set too (1/5 > 2/5 > 3/5 > 4/5)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fix the piece size (a fifth) and count how many are shaded; show 4/5 covers more of the bar than 2/5; separate 'how big each piece' from 'how many pieces'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders the fifths backwards, treating a bigger numerator as smaller

errorPatterns.pattern: Component comparison — compares numerators and denominators independently instead of as one quantity, muddling any set that mixes denominators
errorPatterns.nextMove: Represent each fraction as a length on a common number line and order by position; insist on one quantity per card
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Orders a mixed set by looking only at the top numbers (or only the bottom), ignoring the relationship

responseLevels.gap: Orders unit fractions by denominator size (1/5 largest), or reverses the same-denominator set — whole-number bias runs throughout.
responseLevels.full: Orders both sets correctly and fluently, places them consistently on a number line, and articulates the unifying idea — the denominator sets the piece size (more pieces → smaller each), the numerator counts how many of that piece — transferring to a novel comparison.
responseLevels.partial: Orders unit fractions correctly (1/2…1/5) and same-denominator fractions correctly when each set is done separately, but treats them as two unconnected rules — cannot explain why the denominator direction flips, or falters when sets are mixed or placed on one line.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are four fraction cards: 1/2, 1/5, 1/3, 1/4. Put them in order from LARGEST to smallest. Now here are four more: 3/5, 1/5, 4/5, 2/5 — put these in order from largest to smallest too. As you go, place each fraction on this number line. [Watch how the child orders each set and where they place the cards.]
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Whole-number bias makes a child order the unit fractions 1/5, 1/4, 1/3, 1/2 — the exact reverse of correct — so watching the direction on the unit set exposes it instantly. The same-denominator set is the control: it is ordered by numerator (bigger IS more), so a child who has merely memorised 'bigger bottom = smaller' and reverses everything is caught, distinguishing genuine magnitude reasoning from a reversed rote rule.
